table.text: Participants were recruited via a panel agency No Ties, targeting Dutch adults (18+) who had gambled more than once in the past 12 months.
After the survey (15 minutes), participants were asked for a follow-up assessment (5 minutes).
Participants were asked: "Thinking about your own gambling, how often in the last 12 months has your own gambling led you to...?"
A product breadth score was calculated by summing the number of gambling products participants had used in the last 12 months.
Participants were then classified into two categories: land-based only (0) versus (1) online only or mixed land-based/online.
To assess the understandability of each harm item, participants were asked for each question whether they fully understood it.
Overall, 1045 participants took part in the survey at T0.
In total, 841 participants participated in the follow-up survey (T1).
However, 30 participants were removed for failing attention checks, resulting in a final sample of 811 participants for T1.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: 2025 Applying the gambling harms framework to the Netherlands:  Developing multiple indicators to support assessment of gambling harms
table.research_questions:
# Research question

The main research question is as follows: 

How can gambling harms be better measured [in the Netherlands]? Consider, for example, public health (mental-socio-physical), economic and social costs, and local indicators of damage (e.g. domestic violence, debt, crime).

This effort covers the following sub questions:

- RQ2a: How can measurement of gambling harms be expanded by translating and constructing a Dutch self-report ‘gambling harms measurement inventory’?

- RQ2b: How do the new gambling harms questions perform in a sample of adults who gamble, covering subgroups and various high and low risk gambling products? 

This registration focuses specifically on RQ2b, which relates to the effort to evaluate the performance of the new set of translated/adjusted gambling harms questions for use in Dutch language subjective assessment efforts, e.g. self-report surveys. 

In the effort for RQ2a, we generated two sets of survey items, one for the main study and a brief set of items for the retest follow-up study. The sets of items and scales are briefly listed in this registration for quick referencing, including answer scale for the core questions. 

The full survey meta-data, including exact items and translations to Dutch from English, will be uploaded to the OSF location for this project. A file with the survey logical-flow of the survey will also be uploaded.

# Brief description of sample selection: 

We will field test the Dutch gambling harms items in two distinct samples of adults who gamble: 
We aim to recruit respondents via (A) direct advertising and via (B) a panel study, which reaches people with different patterns of gambling behavior. 

Further detail on recruitment is provided in the design section.

#### Follow up: Retest survey

In both samples, respondents are asked about willingness to participate in the follow-up measurement (the retest-survey). If they are willing to participate, they will be approached with the follow up measurement, 1 week after the initial measurement (Gooding et al., 2025; McLauchlan et al., 2020; Quilty et al., 2015). They will have 1 week to complete the survey, ensuring that the interval between participants varies by no more than 7 days and does not exceed 2 weeks. 

# Hypotheses

The central element in the survey is the set of newly drafted/translated gambling harms items. The harms questions inventory is not foreseen to be a single scale (loading on a single factor), but rather a divergent set of questions that measure a wide range of gambling harms. While many questions can be attributed to defined health subdomains, some individual items might well cover multiple categories.

Unless otherwise stated, the hypotheses relate to all the new harms questions and their various sections. All analyses are planned to be run in the R environment, using a script that will support reproducibility of findings. 

These harms questions cover the following topics: 

- A. 16 items (H1-H21) cover harms across the domains of Financial, Work/Study, Relationships with partner/friends/family, Relations with community, Mental Health, Physical Health, Crime and Other (substance use), with a 4 point answer scale that mirrors the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI) answer scale (never to (almost) always). The answer scale was harmonized to facilitate any potential efforts to an integrated / composite scale out of both PGSI and harms items. 
- B. An additional 5 items (H22-H26) to assess more severe harms across the domains of Financial, Relationships, Work/Study and Crime. These questions are scored yes/no.
- C. 3 final items (H27-H29), preceded by a sensitive topic warning and request for consent to proceed, cover suicidal ideation and suicidal attempts related to gambling. These two harms are asked stepwise: 
   - Suicidal thoughts (yes/no).
   - Suicidal attempts (yes/no).
   - If one or both of the above questions is answered 'yes' > 'To what extent, if at all, was this  
     related to your gambling?" (not at all, a little, a lot). 

The vast majority of the questions have been used in English language form before. Their performance in the Dutch context, after translation, is a topic of interest. A minority of items were adjusted or split into two questions for our survey, so the list does contain new items.

Our exploratory analysis has four specific aims: 

1. Subjective understandability of the Dutch language harms questions by respondents in our samples: are the questions clear? 
2. Response patterns: Evaluating and reporting harms for people of various genders, engaging in various gambling product types.
3. Evaluating the correlations of the harms questions and composites/sums of harms items with relevant indicators that provide information on convergent, divergent and concurrent validity.
4. Test-retest stability: Evaluating the temporal stability of the harms items (test-retest reliability).

### 1. Subjective understandability and missing harms 

E1 Evaluation question Understandability (yes/no - open answer)
- Hypothesis: The majority of participants is expected to find each individual harms question easy to understand (80% or more) in both samples: among panel members as well as among respondents recruited via direct advertising. 

E2 Evaluation question Request for missing harms (open answer)
- Hypothesis: We expect that we did not miss major types of gambling harms in survey construction, given the expansive list of questions, but a minority of respondents (<10%) is expected to supply worthwhile nuance and insight in this question. 

### 2. Response patterns for harms per product type/mode/gender 

P1-P8 Participation in gambling: products, spending, most used product, frequency, etc. and D1-D13 Demographic characteristics
- Hypothesis: Diversity of harms across product and gender. Participation questions will be used to segment our sample into groups based on their gambling participation (P1, P2), online/land-based mode of participation (P3), and most frequently used product form (P5). We expect variation in harms across gambling forms, mode and product breadth (engagement in multiple vs. single form). More specifically, we expect:
      - products with high potential betting frequency and rapid outcome feedback (such as 
        slots and sport betting) to be associated with more (severe) harms than products with 
        lower betting frequency and delayed outcomes such as lotteries;
      - online gambling to be associated with more (severe) harms than land-based only 
         gambling (e.g., Hing et al., 2022);
      - engagement in multiple gambling forms to be associated with more (severe) harms 
         than engagement in a single form (e.g., Miltenburg & Hollander, 2025). 

If subsample sizes per product type allow, results will be split and presented by gender (D4) and/or by product x mode combinations (n ≥ 30). We do not define specific hypotheses per product, product x mode, and product x gender group. These findings serve to establish if the scale behaves in a way that fits with literature based expectations that harms are not equal for each product and group of gamblers.

### 3. Convergent, divergent and concurrent validity

We include multiple scales that provide information that supports assessment of convergent/divergent validity and concurrent validity (Gooding et al., 2025).

F1 Feelings about gambling,  PW1-8 Personal wellbeing questions,  PGSI1-9 Problem gambling severity index & HS1-HS7 Help-seeking behavior for gambling
- Hypothesis: Convergent validity is expected for the overall PGSI scale result, broad personal wellbeing (higher wellbeing associated with more harms), feelings about gambling (more negative feelings associated with more (severe) harms), and help-seeking behavior for gambling (more harms associated with more help-seeking behavior): this will be expressed in correlation values above .60, using appropriate correlation assessment methods for the answer scales on both ends of the comparison. 

P1-P8 participation, including self-assessed money spent, 
- Hypothesis: Concurrent validity is expected for various forms of gambling participation in terms of intensity: deeper engagement in terms of time, product breadth (multiple products regularly engaged in) or financial spend is expected to coincide with more (severe) harms on all domains in a positive correlation, with values above .60, using appropriate correlation assessment methods for the answer scales on both ends of the comparison. 

MH1-5 Mental Health Inventory 5 (1 All the time - 5 Seldom) and the BMI1-6 Bank-Melbourne Institute Reported Financial Wellbeing Scale
- Hypothesis: Domain-specific convergent and divergent validity is expected for mental health items, the wellbeing items, and the financial wellbeing items. We expect mental health items will be positively associated with the mental health relevant gambling harms items. Similarly, the financial wellbeing items are expected to be positively associated with the financially relevant gambling harms items. Additionally, we expect these more specific items to be associated, but to a lesser degree with less domain relevant harms items (divergent validity). 

### 4.Test-retest stability of gambling harms items
 
Measurement 2: Question sets: Test-retest stability of the harms measurement is evaluated in a limited subsample of gambling respondents, consisting of all respondents willing to contribute to this follow-up survey. 

H1-H29, PGSI1-9: The limited second survey will involve all Harms and PGSI items, requests for major changes in life or gambling behavior (C1-C6). 
- Hypothesis:  We expect the measures to be stable over time, as manifested by high correlations (≥ .80) between the first and second survey scores on the described subsets of gambling harms items (A, B & C) and the PGSI. 

E2 Evaluation question Request for missing harms (open answer) [repeated]
- Hypothesis: Repeated question, identical hypothesis to previous: We expect that we did not miss major types of gambling harms in survey construction, given the expansive list of questions, but a minority of respondents (<10%) is expected to supply worthwhile nuance and insight in this question.  

### 5. Factor structure and grouping among the combined harms items and PGSI items 

H1-H26, PGSI1-9
- Hypothesis: we expect items designed to measure specific harm domains (i.e., financial, relationships, work/study, crime, mental health, physical health) to load on coherent factors, while we also expect some items to load on multiple factors. 
- We will visualize the correlational item networks to aid interpretation of item clustering and to further item performance. 

### 6. Enrichment survey items without hypotheses and their purpose

Enrichment and variety: The survey contains a small number of enriching questions, aimed to add more neutral and less harm-oriented questions to provide variety in responding, but also to explore specific topics for optional enrichment of gambling participation groups. 

These questions cover engagement with loot boxes or crypto (P9), for example, or the reasons for gambling (R1-R5). Additionally, we will examine differences in gambling behavior and harms between panel members and respondents recruited via direct advertising. However, this is not the central focus of the current study.
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview:
We will field test the Dutch gambling harms items among adults (18+) who have gambled more than once in the past year. Participants will be recruited through two methods: via (A) a panel study and (B) direct advertising on social media channels (Facebook and Instagram) and Google Ads. 

The notable advantage of recruitment via direct advertising is that we directly recruit active gamblers when they are searching or engaging with gambling related content online. The expectation is that this will recruit people who are more highly engaged in gambling than those who participate in a panel study, potentially also more likely to be an ‘online’ gambler given the nature of the recruitment. However, this recruitment method is more risky given the heavy advertisement on the gambling market and future (unknown) conversion success in the recruitment.

### Follow-up: retest survey

In both samples, respondents are asked about willingness to participate in the follow-up measurement (the retest-survey). If they are willing to participate, they will be approached with the follow up measurement, 1 2 weeks after the initial measurement (Gooding et al., 2025; McLauchlan et al., 2020; Quilty et al., 2015). They will have 1 week to complete the survey, ensuring that the interval between participants varies by no more than 7 days and does not exceed 2 weeks.

table.data_collection_procedures: Inclusion criteria are adults (18+) who have gambled more than once in the past 12 months. Participants will be recruited through two methods: recruitment via a panel agency and recruitment via online advertisements. See ‘Study Design’ for more details about the recruitment process. The initial survey will take approximately 30 minutes to complete, and the follow-up survey approximately 10 minutes. At the end of the initial survey, participants will be asked to indicate their willingness to take part in the follow-up assessment and to share their email address for one-time use only (only for participants recruited via advertising; for panel members, their email address is already known to the panel agency). Participants who consent to the follow-up, will receive a link to the follow-up survey one week after completing the initial survey. They will have one week to complete it, and a reminder will be sent in this period. Both surveys will be administered online. Panel members will receive points as a reward for completing the survey according to the panel provider’s guidelines. Once a minimum number of points is reached, panel members can redeem their points for a Bol.com giftcard. Participants recruited via advertising will receive a Bol.com giftcard of €5 for each completed survey if they provide an email address. Participants will provide active informed consent prior to the survey, with clear information about how their data will be stored and used.
table.sample_size:
We aim to recruit a sufficiently large and diverse sample to allow robust evaluation of the gambling harms questions. A key requirement is adequate representation across different gambling product categories, as gambling harms are known to vary by product type. To achieve stable estimates and allow for subgroup comparisons, we strive for a minimum sample size of N=500 for the first measurement, with a minimum of 50 respondents per product category (sports/soccer betting; slots/electronic and digitized gambling machines; casino-games and table card games; poker, betting on animal races/horses; bingo; scratch cards; lotteries; and an ‘other’ category). A maximum of 50 respondents will be allowed for those who participate exclusively in lotteries, as people who only engage in lotteries are generally at lower risk of gambling harms. Coverage across product type will be assessed during data collection to see if any modification of advertising is necessary.

For the test-retest, we strive for a minimum sample size of N=200.
table.sample_size_rationale: A power analysis is not necessary for this study, as this study focuses on evaluating how new gambling harms questions perform instead of estimating effects. Existing literature recommends a sample size of at least 500-600 for pilot testing measurement instruments (Van Rooij et al., 2017). The sample size will be constrained by the available budget for recruitment and participant incentives.

table.indices:
For measures with multiple items, scale scores will be constructed. 

P1 Product breadth last 12 months
For this variable, P1 (participation in different gambling forms) will be used:
Coding for each gambling form:
    0 = did not participate ever
    1 = participated longer than 12 months ago
    2 = participated in the last 12 months
Scores will be recoded into a dummy variable: combining ‘did not participate ever’ + ‘participated longer than 12 months ago’ = 0, ‘participated in the last 12 months’ = 1. 
Scale score: sum of scores across all gambling forms.

table.statistical_tests:
The harms questions inventory is not foreseen to be unidimensional, but rather a set of questions that measure a wide range of harms, following the approach of the UK Gambling Commission (Gambling Commission, 2024). Analysis includes descriptive analyses to evaluate subjective understanding, comparing responses to questions among different types of people and different gambling products, validity assessment (convergent, divergent and concurrent validity), test-retest stability and exploratory factor analysis. 

### Understandability
We will evaluate understandability by obtaining the percentage of respondents who report that the question is easy to understand. This will be presented for each individual harms question. The descriptives will be reported separately for the two recruitment samples.  

### Missing harms
For evaluation on missing harms, open responses will be analyzed to assess whether respondents suggest any substantive harm types not included in the survey or nuance within existing categories. The main descriptive will be the percentage of respondents who suggest missing harms/nuances within presented harms. We will also provide a qualitative summary of the nature of the suggestions.

### Response patterns among different groups
To evaluate response patterns among different groups, subgroups will be defined based on (a) primary gambling form (e.g., slots, lotteries, poker, etc.), (b) product breadth (engagement in multiple vs. single gambling forms), (c) gambling mode (online only, offline only, mixed), and (d) a combination of form and mode if sample size allows (n ≥ 30; e.g., online slots, offline poker etc.). If sample size allows (n ≥ 30), groups will also be split by gender. For each subgroup, we will obtain descriptives, both at the level of scale scores for each harms subset as well as for each harms domain. Descriptive statistics include means, standard deviations and distribution of responses. Prevalence of endorsement for individual harms items will also be calculated. Group differences will be examined using ANOVA or non-parametric equivalents with post-hoc tests (for comparing 3+ groups on continuous outcomes), t-tests or non-parametric equivalents (for comparing two groups on continuous outcomes), and chi-square tests (for comparing 2+ groups on a binary outcome).  

### Convergent, divergent and concucrrent validity
To evaluate convergent, divergent and concurrent validity, we will compute bivariate correlations between gambling harms and external constructs. The choice of correlation method (Pearson, Spearman, or polychoric) will depend on the distribution of the data and the type of measurement scales (e.g., ordinal, continuous) of the variables being compared. 

- Convergent validity
  To evaluate convergent validity, correlations will be computed between each subset of   
  gambling harms and (a) the overall PGSI scale, (b) feelings about gambling, and (c) personal 
  wellbeing. Positive correlations above .60 will be considered as demonstrating sufficient 
  convergent validity. 

- Concurrent validity
  To evaluate concurrent validity, correlations will be computed between gambling harms  
  and measures of gambling participation intensity, including (a) frequency, (b) product 
  breadth, and (c) money spent on gambling. Positive correlations above .60 will be 
  considered as demonstrating sufficient concurrent validity. 

- Domain-specific convergent/divergent validity 
  To evaluate convergent/divergent validity of each harms domain, correlations will be 
  computed between each harms domain and (a) financial wellbeing and (b) mental health. 
  We expect associations to be stronger in case of conceptual overlap (e.g. financial gambling 
  harms with financial wellbeing, mental health related gambling harms with mental health), 
  providing evidence for both convergent and divergent validity. 

### Test-retest stability
To evaluate test-retest stability, bivariate correlations will be computed between scale scores from the first and second survey for the gambling harms subsets (A, B & C) and the PGSI. Correlations of .80 or higher will be considered evidence for sufficient stability over time. The choice of correlation method (Pearson, Spearman, or polychoric) will depend on the measurement level of the scales and the distribution of the data. 

### Exploratory factor analysis
Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) will be used to examine the factor structure and grouping of the harms and PGSI items. Oblique rotation will be used to allow factors to correlate, reflecting the expectation that harm domains are related. Factor extraction will be based on multiple criteria, including eigenvalues > 1, scree plot inspection, and factor loadings. In addition to EFA, we will construct and visualize the correlational item networks to aid interpretation of item clustering and to further explore item performance.
table.inference_criteria: In statistical tests, a two-sided significance level of α = 0.05 will be applied.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
The survey contains two attentiveness checks that supplement the more visualized checks of the panel agency (which also processes the advertising recruited respondents) that seek to discourage automated bot responses. Cases will be excluded from the analyses when they fail both attentiveness checks. When respondents fail one of the two attentiveness checks, we will inspect response patterns: cases showing careless response patterns will be excluded. Similarly, for non-complete cases (respondents who did not finish the survey), we will also inspect their response pattern to identify nonserious responding. 

For evaluation of test-retest stability of the gambling harms sets and the PGSI, participants who report any major changes in life or gambling behavior since the first measurement wave will be excluded from the test-retest analyses.
table.missing_data_handling:
In the survey platform, participants are required to provide a response to each item in order to proceed, to limit item-level missingness within completed sections of the survey. 

Missing data will arise in cases where respondents discontinue participation partway through the survey, resulting in mostly unit nonresponse from the point of dropout onward. However, we expect this to be minimal. 

Depending on the extent and nature of missing data, we will determine the most appropriate method for handling missing responses. We will evaluate and report on potentially selective non-response across demographics characteristics. Besides, for participants with incomplete data, we will examine their response patterns to assess whether the data indicate careless answering. 

For the planned follow-up test, we expect that only a small proportion of participants will take part. For the test-retest analysis, only available cases (i.e. participants who also completed the follow-up survey) will be used. Again, as the characteristics of the full sample are known, we will evaluate and report on potentially selective non-response across demographics characteristics.
table.exploratory_analyses: To evaluate response patterns among different groups, as well as the factor structure and grouping of the harms and PGSI items, a (partially) exploratory approach will be employed. For a detailed description, see the section ‘Statistical models’.

The main research question is as follows:

How can gambling harms be better measured [in the Netherlands]? Consider, for example, public health (mental-socio-physical), economic and social costs, and local indicators of damage (e.g. domestic violence, debt, crime).

This effort covers the following sub questions:

- RQ2a: How can measurement of gambling harms be expanded by translating and constructing a Dutch self-report ‘gambling harms measurement inventory’?

- RQ2b: How do the new gambling harms questions perform in a sample of adults who gamble, covering subgroups and various high and low risk gambling products?

This registration focuses specifically on RQ2b, which relates to the effort to evaluate the performance of the new set of translated/adjusted gambling harms questions for use in Dutch language subjective assessment efforts, e.g. self-report surveys.

In the effort for RQ2a, we generated two sets of survey items, one for the main study and a brief set of items for the retest follow-up study. The sets of items and scales are briefly listed in this registration for quick referencing, including answer scale for the core questions.

The full survey meta-data, including exact items and translations to Dutch from English, will be uploaded to the OSF location for this project. A file with the survey logical-flow of the survey will also be uploaded.

# Brief description of sample selection:

We will field test the Dutch gambling harms items in two distinct samples of adults who gamble:
We aim to recruit respondents via (A) direct advertising and via (B) a panel study, which reaches people with different patterns of gambling behavior.

Further detail on recruitment is provided in the design section.

#### Follow up: Retest survey

In both samples, respondents are asked about willingness to participate in the follow-up measurement (the retest-survey). If they are willing to participate, they will be approached with the follow up measurement, 1 week after the initial measurement (Gooding et al., 2025; McLauchlan et al., 2020; Quilty et al., 2015). They will have 1 week to complete the survey, ensuring that the interval between participants varies by no more than 7 days and does not exceed 2 weeks.

# Hypotheses

The central element in the survey is the set of newly drafted/translated gambling harms items. The harms questions inventory is not foreseen to be a single scale (loading on a single factor), but rather a divergent set of questions that measure a wide range of gambling harms. While many questions can be attributed to defined health subdomains, some individual items might well cover multiple categories.

Unless otherwise stated, the hypotheses relate to all the new harms questions and their various sections. All analyses are planned to be run in the R environment, using a script that will support reproducibility of findings.

These harms questions cover the following topics:

- A. 16 items (H1-H21) cover harms across the domains of Financial, Work/Study, Relationships with partner/friends/family, Relations with community, Mental Health, Physical Health, Crime and Other (substance use), with a 4 point answer scale that mirrors the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI) answer scale (never to (almost) always). The answer scale was harmonized to facilitate any potential efforts to an integrated / composite scale out of both PGSI and harms items.
- B. An additional 5 items (H22-H26) to assess more severe harms across the domains of Financial, Relationships, Work/Study and Crime. These questions are scored yes/no.
- C. 3 final items (H27-H29), preceded by a sensitive topic warning and request for consent to proceed, cover suicidal ideation and suicidal attempts related to gambling. These two harms are asked stepwise:
- Suicidal thoughts (yes/no).
- Suicidal attempts (yes/no).
- If one or both of the above questions is answered 'yes' > 'To what extent, if at all, was this
related to your gambling?\" (not at all, a little, a lot).

The vast majority of the questions have been used in English language form before. Their performance in the Dutch context, after translation, is a topic of interest. A minority of items were adjusted or split into two questions for our survey, so the list does contain new items.

Our exploratory analysis has four specific aims:

1. Subjective understandability of the Dutch language harms questions by respondents in our samples: are the questions clear?
2. Response patterns: Evaluating and reporting harms for people of various genders, engaging in various gambling product types.
3. Evaluating the correlations of the harms questions and composites/sums of harms items with relevant indicators that provide information on convergent, divergent and concurrent validity.
4. Test-retest stability: Evaluating the temporal stability of the harms items (test-retest reliability).

### 1. Subjective understandability and missing harms

E1 Evaluation question Understandability (yes/no - open answer)
- Hypothesis: The majority of participants is expected to find each individual harms question easy to understand (80% or more) in both samples: among panel members as well as among respondents recruited via direct advertising.

E2 Evaluation question Request for missing harms (open answer)
- Hypothesis: We expect that we did not miss major types of gambling harms in survey construction, given the expansive list of questions, but a minority of respondents (<10%) is expected to supply worthwhile nuance and insight in this question.

### 2. Response patterns for harms per product type/mode/gender

P1-P8 Participation in gambling: products, spending, most used product, frequency, etc. and D1-D13 Demographic characteristics
- Hypothesis: Diversity of harms across product and gender. Participation questions will be used to segment our sample into groups based on their gambling participation (P1, P2), online/land-based mode of participation (P3), and most frequently used product form (P5). We expect variation in harms across gambling forms, mode and product breadth (engagement in multiple vs. single form). More specifically, we expect:
- products with high potential betting frequency and rapid outcome feedback (such as
slots and sport betting) to be associated with more (severe) harms than products with
lower betting frequency and delayed outcomes such as lotteries;
- online gambling to be associated with more (severe) harms than land-based only
gambling (e.g., Hing et al., 2022);
- engagement in multiple gambling forms to be associated with more (severe) harms
than engagement in a single form (e.g., Miltenburg & Hollander, 2025).

If subsample sizes per product type allow, results will be split and presented by gender (D4) and/or by product x mode combinations (n ≥ 30). We do not define specific hypotheses per product, product x mode, and product x gender group. These findings serve to establish if the scale behaves in a way that fits with literature based expectations that harms are not equal for each product and group of gamblers.

### 3. Convergent, divergent and concurrent validity

We include multiple scales that provide information that supports assessment of convergent/divergent validity and concurrent validity (Gooding et al., 2025).

F1 Feelings about gambling, PW1-8 Personal wellbeing questions, PGSI1-9 Problem gambling severity index & HS1-HS7 Help-seeking behavior for gambling
- Hypothesis: Convergent validity is expected for the overall PGSI scale result, broad personal wellbeing (higher wellbeing associated with more harms), feelings about gambling (more negative feelings associated with more (severe) harms), and help-seeking behavior for gambling (more harms associated with more help-seeking behavior): this will be expressed in correlation values above .60, using appropriate correlation assessment methods for the answer scales on both ends of the comparison.

P1-P8 participation, including self-assessed money spent,
- Hypothesis: Concurrent validity is expected for various forms of gambling participation in terms of intensity: deeper engagement in terms of time, product breadth (multiple products regularly engaged in) or financial spend is expected to coincide with more (severe) harms on all domains in a positive correlation, with values above .60, using appropriate correlation assessment methods for the answer scales on both ends of the comparison.

MH1-5 Mental Health Inventory 5 (1 All the time - 5 Seldom) and the BMI1-6 Bank-Melbourne Institute Reported Financial Wellbeing Scale
- Hypothesis: Domain-specific convergent and divergent validity is expected for mental health items, the wellbeing items, and the financial wellbeing items. We expect mental health items will be positively associated with the mental health relevant gambling harms items. Similarly, the financial wellbeing items are expected to be positively associated with the financially relevant gambling harms items. Additionally, we expect these more specific items to be associated, but to a lesser degree with less domain relevant harms items (divergent validity).

### 4.Test-retest stability of gambling harms items

Measurement 2: Question sets: Test-retest stability of the harms measurement is evaluated in a limited subsample of gambling respondents, consisting of all respondents willing to contribute to this follow-up survey.

H1-H29, PGSI1-9: The limited second survey will involve all Harms and PGSI items, requests for major changes in life or gambling behavior (C1-C6).
- Hypothesis: We expect the measures to be stable over time, as manifested by high correlations (≥ .80) between the first and second survey scores on the described subsets of gambling harms items (A, B & C) and the PGSI.

E2 Evaluation question Request for missing harms (open answer) [repeated]
- Hypothesis: Repeated question, identical hypothesis to previous: We expect that we did not miss major types of gambling harms in survey construction, given the expansive list of questions, but a minority of respondents (<10%) is expected to supply worthwhile nuance and insight in this question.

### 5. Factor structure and grouping among the combined harms items and PGSI items

H1-H26, PGSI1-9
- Hypothesis: we expect items designed to measure specific harm domains (i.e., financial, relationships, work/study, crime, mental health, physical health) to load on coherent factors, while we also expect some items to load on multiple factors.
- We will visualize the correlational item networks to aid interpretation of item clustering and to further item performance.

### 6. Enrichment survey items without hypotheses and their purpose

Enrichment and variety: The survey contains a small number of enriching questions, aimed to add more neutral and less harm-oriented questions to provide variety in responding, but also to explore specific topics for optional enrichment of gambling participation groups.

These questions cover engagement with loot boxes or crypto (P9), for example, or the reasons for gambling (R1-R5). Additionally, we will examine differences in gambling behavior and harms between panel members and respondents recruited via direct advertising. However, this is not the central focus of the current study.", "Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.", "No blinding is involved in this study.", "n/a", "We will field test the Dutch gambling harms items among adults (18+) who have gambled more than once in the past year. Participants will be recruited through two methods: via (A) a panel study and (B) direct advertising on social media channels (Facebook and Instagram) and Google Ads.

The notable advantage of recruitment via direct advertising is that we directly recruit active gamblers when they are searching or engaging with gambling related content online. The expectation is that this will recruit people who are more highly engaged in gambling than those who participate in a panel study, potentially also more likely to be an ‘online’ gambler given the nature of the recruitment. However, this recruitment method is more risky given the heavy advertisement on the gambling market and future (unknown) conversion success in the recruitment.

### Follow-up: retest survey

In both samples, respondents are asked about willingness to participate in the follow-up measurement (the retest-survey). If they are willing to participate, they will be approached with the follow up measurement, 1 2 weeks after the initial measurement (Gooding et al., 2025; McLauchlan et al., 2020; Quilty et al., 2015). Participants will be recruited through two methods: recruitment via a panel agency and recruitment via online advertisements. See ‘Study Design’ for more details about the recruitment process. The initial survey will take approximately 30 minutes to complete, and the follow-up survey approximately 10 minutes. At the end of the initial survey, participants will be asked to indicate their willingness to take part in the follow-up assessment and to share their email address for one-time use only (only for participants recruited via advertising; for panel members, their email address is already known to the panel agency). Participants who consent to the follow-up, will receive a link to the follow-up survey one week after completing the initial survey. They will have one week to complete it, and a reminder will be sent in this period. Both surveys will be administered online. Panel members will receive points as a reward for completing the survey according to the panel provider’s guidelines. Once a minimum number of points is reached, panel members can redeem their points for a Bol.com giftcard. Participants recruited via advertising will receive a Bol.com giftcard of €5 for each completed survey if they provide an email address. Participants will provide active informed consent prior to the survey, with clear information about how their data will be stored and used.", "We aim to recruit a sufficiently large and diverse sample to allow robust evaluation of the gambling harms questions. A key requirement is adequate representation across different gambling product categories, as gambling harms are known to vary by product type. To achieve stable estimates and allow for subgroup comparisons, we strive for a minimum sample size of N=500 for the first measurement, with a minimum of 50 respondents per product category (sports/soccer betting; slots/electronic and digitized gambling machines; casino-games and table card games; poker, betting on animal races/horses; bingo; scratch cards; lotteries; and an ‘other’ category). A maximum of 50 respondents will be allowed for those who participate exclusively in lotteries, as people who only engage in lotteries are generally at lower risk of gambling harms. Coverage across product type will be assessed during data collection to see if any modification of advertising is necessary.

Analysis includes descriptive analyses to evaluate subjective understanding, comparing responses to questions among different types of people and different gambling products, validity assessment (convergent, divergent and concurrent validity), test-retest stability and exploratory factor analysis.

### Understandability
We will evaluate understandability by obtaining the percentage of respondents who report that the question is easy to understand. This will be presented for each individual harms question. The descriptives will be reported separately for the two recruitment samples.

### Missing harms
For evaluation on missing harms, open responses will be analyzed to assess whether respondents suggest any substantive harm types not included in the survey or nuance within existing categories. The main descriptive will be the percentage of respondents who suggest missing harms/nuances within presented harms. We will also provide a qualitative summary of the nature of the suggestions.

### Response patterns among different groups
To evaluate response patterns among different groups, subgroups will be defined based on (a) primary gambling form (e.g., slots, lotteries, poker, etc.), (b) product breadth (engagement in multiple vs. single gambling forms), (c) gambling mode (online only, offline only, mixed), and (d) a combination of form and mode if sample size allows (n ≥ 30; e.g., online slots, offline poker etc.). If sample size allows (n ≥ 30), groups will also be split by gender. For each subgroup, we will obtain descriptives, both at the level of scale scores for each harms subset as well as for each harms domain. Descriptive statistics include means, standard deviations and distribution of responses. Prevalence of endorsement for individual harms items will also be calculated. Group differences will be examined using ANOVA or non-parametric equivalents with post-hoc tests (for comparing 3+ groups on continuous outcomes), t-tests or non-parametric equivalents (for comparing two groups on continuous outcomes), and chi-square tests (for comparing 2+ groups on a binary outcome).

### Convergent, divergent and concucrrent validity
To evaluate convergent, divergent and concurrent validity, we will compute bivariate correlations between gambling harms and external constructs. The choice of correlation method (Pearson, Spearman, or polychoric) will depend on the distribution of the data and the type of measurement scales (e.g., ordinal, continuous) of the variables being compared.

- Convergent validity
To evaluate convergent validity, correlations will be computed between each subset of
gambling harms and (a) the overall PGSI scale, (b) feelings about gambling, and (c) personal
wellbeing. Positive correlations above .60 will be considered as demonstrating sufficient
convergent validity.

- Concurrent validity
To evaluate concurrent validity, correlations will be computed between gambling harms
and measures of gambling participation intensity, including (a) frequency, (b) product
breadth, and (c) money spent on gambling. Positive correlations above .60 will be
considered as demonstrating sufficient concurrent validity.

- Domain-specific convergent/divergent validity
To evaluate convergent/divergent validity of each harms domain, correlations will be
computed between each harms domain and (a) financial wellbeing and (b) mental health.
We expect associations to be stronger in case of conceptual overlap (e.g. financial gambling
harms with financial wellbeing, mental health related gambling harms with mental health),
providing evidence for both convergent and divergent validity.

### Test-retest stability
To evaluate test-retest stability, bivariate correlations will be computed between scale scores from the first and second survey for the gambling harms subsets (A, B & C) and the PGSI. Correlations of .80 or higher will be considered evidence for sufficient stability over time. The choice of correlation method (Pearson, Spearman, or polychoric) will depend on the measurement level of the scales and the distribution of the data.

### Exploratory factor analysis
Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) will be used to examine the factor structure and grouping of the harms and PGSI items. Oblique rotation will be used to allow factors to correlate, reflecting the expectation that harm domains are related. Factor extraction will be based on multiple criteria, including eigenvalues > 1, scree plot inspection, and factor loadings. In addition to EFA, we will construct and visualize the correlational item networks to aid interpretation of item clustering and to further explore item performance.", "n/a", "In statistical tests, a two-sided significance level of α = 0.05 will be applied.", "The survey contains two attentiveness checks that supplement the more visualized checks of the panel agency (which also processes the advertising recruited respondents) that seek to discourage automated bot responses. Similarly, for non-complete cases (respondents who did not finish the survey), we will also inspect their response pattern to identify nonserious responding.

For evaluation of test-retest stability of the gambling harms sets and the PGSI, participants who report any major changes in life or gambling behavior since the first measurement wave will be excluded from the test-retest analyses.", "In the survey platform, participants are required to provide a response to each item in order to proceed, to limit item-level missingness within completed sections of the survey.

Missing data will arise in cases where respondents discontinue participation partway through the survey, resulting in mostly unit nonresponse from the point of dropout onward. However, we expect this to be minimal.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 2023 columns across 15 data files.
#### Issues Identified

137 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding

2350 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **1595 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 6 of 15 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 3 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).

-  21 installable dependencies detected.

live_data_statements: Participants were recruited via a panel agency No Ties, targeting Dutch adults (18+) who had gambled more than once in the past 12 months.
After the survey (15 minutes), participants were asked for a follow-up assessment (5 minutes).
Participants were asked: "Thinking about your own gambling, how often in the last 12 months has your own gambling led you to...?"
A product breadth score was calculated by summing the number of gambling products participants had used in the last 12 months.
Participants were then classified into two categories: land-based only (0) versus (1) online only or mixed land-based/online.
To assess the understandability of each harm item, participants were asked for each question whether they fully understood it.
Overall, 1045 participants took part in the survey at T0.
In total, 841 participants participated in the follow-up survey (T1).
However, 30 participants were removed for failing attention checks, resulting in a final sample of 811 participants for T1.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 3 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:3, File = c("ZonMw Harms_cleaning.Rmd", 
"ZonMw Harms_analyses_panel.Rmd", "ZonMw Harms_description panel sample.Rmd"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "ZonMw Harms_cleaning.Rmd", "ZonMw Harms_cleaning.Rmd"
), Basis = c("none", "dependency", "dependency")), row.names = c(NA, 
-3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**4 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `Data_raw/ZonMwHarms_T0_raw.sav` to `../Data/Raw data/ZonMwHarms_T0_raw.sav` (in ZonMw Harms_cleaning.Rmd); `Data_raw/ZonMwHarms_T1_raw.sav` to `../Data/Raw data/ZonMwHarms_T1_raw.sav` (in ZonMw Harms_cleaning.Rmd); `Data_processed/ZonMwHarms_T0T1_analysisready.sav` to `../Data/Final data/ZonMwHarms_T0T1_analysisready.sav` (in ZonMw Harms_description panel sample.Rmd); `ZonMwHarms_T0T1_analysisready.sav` to `../Data/Final data/ZonMwHarms_T0T1_analysisready.sav` (in ZonMw Harms_analyses_panel.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `renamed variables, labels and values.xlsx`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 3 scripts: 2 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
"ran_ok", "ran_ok"), Detail = c("runtime", "", ""), "Time (s)" = c(5.2, 
17.3, 5)), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

9 calls to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. > run_harms_nb <- function(outcome, predictors, data, domain_label) {
````
> 
>   results <- lapply(predictors, function(var) {
> 
>     model <- glm.nb(
>       as.formula(
>         paste(outcome, "~ relevel(factor(", var, "), ref = '0')", sep = "")
>       ),
>       data = data
>     )
> 
>     tidy(model, conf.int = TRUE) |>
>       mutate(
>         IRR = exp(estimate), 
>         IRR_low = exp(conf.low),
>         IRR_high = exp(conf.high),
>         Predictor = domain_label,
>         Harm_item = var
>       )
>   }) |>
>     bind_rows()
> 
>   results |>
>     dplyr::select(Predictor, Harm_item, term, estimate, IRR, IRR_low, IRR_high, std.error, p.value) |>
>     mutate(
>       across(c(estimate, IRR, IRR_low, IRR_high, std.error), ~ round(.x, 3)),
>       p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3, eps = .001)
>     )
> }

> run_severeharms_lm <- function(outcome, predictors, data, domain_label) {
> 
>   results <- lapply(predictors, function(var) {
> 
>     model <- lm(
>       as.formula(
>         paste(outcome, "~ relevel(factor(", var, "), ref = '0')", sep = "")
>       ),
>       data = data
>     )
> 
>     tidy(model, conf.int = TRUE) |>
>       mutate(
>         Predictor = domain_label,
>         Harm_item = var
>       )
>   }) |>
>     bind_rows()
> 
>   results |>
>     dplyr::select(Predictor, Harm_item, term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, std.error, p.value) |>
>     mutate(
>       across(c(estimate, conf.low, conf.high, std.error), ~ round(.x, 3)),
>       p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3, eps = .001)
>     )
> }

> run_harms_nb <- function(outcome, predictors, data, domain_label) {
> 
>   results <- lapply(predictors, function(var) {
> 
>     model <- glm.nb(
>       as.formula(
>         paste(outcome, "~ relevel(factor(", var, "), ref = '0')", sep = "")
>       ),
>       data = data
>     )
> 
>     tidy(model, conf.int = TRUE) |>
>       mutate(
>         IRR = exp(estimate), 
>         IRR_low = exp(conf.low),
>         IRR_high = exp(conf.high),
>         Predictor = domain_label,
>         Harm_item = var
>       )
>   }) |>
>     bind_rows()
> 
>   results |>
>     dplyr::select(Predictor, Harm_item, term, estimate, IRR, IRR_low, IRR_high, std.error, p.value) |>
>     mutate(
>       across(c(estimate, IRR, IRR_low, IRR_high, std.error), ~ round(.x, 3)),
>       p.value = format.pval(p.value, digits = 3, eps = .001)
>     )
> }
````

#### Reported vs. reproduced
106 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 12 matched (0 fully, 12 partially) — 11.3% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The "Plausible" column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output's own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.
#### SPSS data without syntax

An SPSS data file (`.sav`/`.por`) is present but **no SPSS syntax file (`.sps`) was found**, so the analysis that produced the results cannot be reproduced from the deposit. This is treated as a reproducibility failure (red). Consider depositing the analysis in **jamovi** (`.omv`) or **JASP** (`.jasp`) instead: these formats store the data and the analyses together in one file, so the results are reproducible from the file itself.

text.text: Acknowledgement.
We thank Jeroen Wisselink (Stichting Informatie Voorziening Zorg) for his involvement in the Dutch gambling harms project, as well as gambling (harms) experts Dr.
Marionneau, Dr.
Reith, and Dr.
Volberg.
We also thank the various involved stakeholders in the Dutch gambling landscape and the people with lived experience who evaluated our materials.
There has been a widespread growth in legal gambling opportunities, including in the Netherlands.
However, gambling can lead to adverse consequences for individuals, families, communities and the wider society, so-called gambling harms [1] [2] [3] [4] .
text.formatted: However, gambling can lead to adverse consequences for individuals, families, communities and the wider society, so-called gambling harms <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> .

text.text: Recognizing these risks, the Lancet Public Health Commission on gambling and the World Health Organisation (WHO) emphasize the importance of adopting a public health approach to gambling regulation and the prevention of gambling harms 3, 5 .
text.formatted: Recognizing these risks, the Lancet Public Health Commission on gambling and the World Health Organisation (WHO) emphasize the importance of adopting a public health approach to gambling regulation and the prevention of gambling harms <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr">5</ref> .

text.text: A public health approach broadens the scope: It recognizes that harms occur even in the absence of a gambling disorder.
Harms can affect both the individual and their contacts.

Importantly, gambling harms exist along a continuum, ranging from mild and short-lived impacts to severe and enduring problems that may persist after gambling has stopped and may affect multiple generations.
Langham et  al. (2016) 1 provided one of the first systematic conceptual frameworks designed to characterize the manifestation and breadth of gambling-related harms.
text.formatted: Langham et  <ref type="formula">al. (2016)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> provided one of the first systematic conceptual frameworks designed to characterize the manifestation and breadth of gambling-related harms.

text.text: Their framework organized harms into seven domains (financial; relationships; emotional/psychological; health; cultural harm; performance at work/study; criminal) and considered their effects on people who gamble, affected others, and the wider community.

This framework provided the basis for the 72-item checklist covering a broad range of harm and briefer tools, including the 10-item Short Gambling Harm Screen (SGHS) 6 , SGHS-18 7 and the 7-item Domain-General Gambling Harm Scale 8. 4 subsequently proposed a parsimonious Framework for Action, organizing gambling-related harms into three interconnected domains: resources, relationships, and health.
text.formatted: This framework provided the basis for the 72-item checklist covering a broad range of harm and briefer tools, including the 10-item Short Gambling Harm Screen (SGHS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">6</ref> , SGHS-18 <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">7</ref> and the 7-item Domain-General Gambling Harm Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">8</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> subsequently proposed a parsimonious Framework for Action, organizing gambling-related harms into three interconnected domains: resources, relationships, and health.

text.text: The resources domain encompasses consequences relating to money and debt, employment, and crime; the relationships domain incorporates impacts on partners, family, friends, and communities; and the health domain includes physical health, psychological distress, and mental health.

This framework was explicitly developed to support the assessment and monitoring of gambling-related harms and has subsequently informed the construction of population-survey questions, which have been developed by the British Gambling Commission for yearly inclusion in the Gambling Survey for Great Britain 9.
text.formatted: This framework was explicitly developed to support the assessment and monitoring of gambling-related harms and has subsequently informed the construction of population-survey questions, which have been developed by the British Gambling Commission for yearly inclusion in the Gambling Survey for Great Britain <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">9</ref>.

text.text: Currently, the Netherlands lacks a standardized Dutch-language questionnaire to measure gambling harms.
Monitoring efforts largely rely on the prevalence of so-called problem gambling or gambling disorder, which capture symptoms of disorder and only a few negative consequences from gambling.

As such, they cannot serve as adequate proxies for the overall societal burden of gambling 1, 10 To address this, the current study aimed to develop and validate a set of questions spanning all gambling harms domains relevant to the Dutch context.
text.formatted: As such, they cannot serve as adequate proxies for the overall societal burden of gambling <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">10</ref> To address this, the current study aimed to develop and validate a set of questions spanning all gambling harms domains relevant to the Dutch context.

text.text: We first evaluated the performance of 26 items, covering eight harm domains across a range of measures.
Secondly, we evaluated reduction into a brief inventory.

In a first step, the performance of each item was evaluated by testing the understandability of the item, the convergent validity, test-retest stability and adequate content coverage of the item pool.
Specifically, to test convergent validity of the measured gambling-related harms, we expected the scores to vary with patterns of gambling involvement, gambling severity and wellbeing.

Gambling products that allow frequent, repeated betting and rapid feedback, such as electronic gaming machines and some forms of sports betting, have been associated with greater problemgambling severity and psychological distress 7, 11 .
text.formatted: Gambling products that allow frequent, repeated betting and rapid feedback, such as electronic gaming machines and some forms of sports betting, have been associated with greater problemgambling severity and psychological distress <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">11</ref> .

text.text: Moreover, online and mixed-mode gambling, as well as participation in multiple gambling products, are also associated with gambling involvement and harm 12, 13 .
text.formatted: Moreover, online and mixed-mode gambling, as well as participation in multiple gambling products, are also associated with gambling involvement and harm <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">13</ref> .

text.text: Furthermore, gambling harm has been positively associated with problem-gambling severity and negatively associated with financial, personal, and psychological wellbeing 1, 8 .
text.formatted: Furthermore, gambling harm has been positively associated with problem-gambling severity and negatively associated with financial, personal, and psychological wellbeing <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">8</ref> .

text.text: These hypotheses follow: Higher scores on each individual harm item will be associated with gambling behaviour.
Specifically, higher harm scores will be associated with: i.
the use of gambling products with high potential betting frequency and rapid outcome feedback, ii.
online or mixed-mode gambling compared with land-based-only, iii. the use of multiple gambling product types.

Higher scores on each individual harm item will be associated with problematic gambling and wellbeing constructs, such that higher harm scores will be associated with: i. with higher levels of problematic gambling, ii.
with lower financial wellbeing, iii.
with lower personal wellbeing, and iv.
more mental health problems.
In a second step, the best performing item for each domain is selected, using the preceding findings.
These items are combined in a brief harms questionnaire.
Such a brief set has better chances of successful, broad, adoption into (population) research practice in the Dutch context, as surveys are limited in space.
