text.text: To develop a Dutch inventory of gambling-related harms, we first conducted a focused literature search on existing conceptual gambling harms frameworks to identify relevant harm domains published between 2021 and 2025 (A1). 2021 was chosen as the start date because prior work had already synthesised frameworks available by that date 2 .
text.formatted: To develop a Dutch inventory of gambling-related harms, we first conducted a focused literature search on existing conceptual gambling harms frameworks to identify relevant harm domains published between 2021 and 2025 (A1). 2021 was chosen as the start date because prior work had already synthesised frameworks available by that date <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: No new relevant frameworks were identified.
Thus, the seven harm domains identified by Marionneau et al. (financial, relational, emotional and psychological, health, cultural, work/study and crime) formed the basis of our work.
To evaluate local relevance, the domains and harms were translated to Dutch.
An in-person meeting was held with 13 local stakeholders, including the regulator, government, individuals with lived-experience, and health professionals.
This included both anonymous consultation and open discussion.
Stakeholders expressed agreement with the domains (A2).
Item development began by using the 14 questions measuring gambling-related adverse consequences developed for the Gambling Survey for Great Britain (GSGB) 9 .
text.formatted: Item development began by using the 14 questions measuring gambling-related adverse consequences developed for the Gambling Survey for Great Britain (GSGB) <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">9</ref> .

text.text: These questions were then reviewed to fill gaps in domain coverage and ensure each item focused on a single component of harm (A3).

Following the GSGB approach, we developed two question sets: One set (hereafter: frequency-based harms) comprises 21 items and uses a 4-point response scale measuring the frequency of (recurring) harms.
The other set (hereafter: event-based harms) comprises 5 items and uses a binary response scale (yes/no), assessing experience of harmful events.
Each of the 7 domains was represented by at least two frequency-based harm items.
Three experts reviewed the items, resulting in minor clarity adjustments (A4).
Items were translated from English to Dutch using generative artificial intelligence (ChatGPT 4o) and a human quality check 15, 16 .
text.formatted: Items were translated from English to Dutch using generative artificial intelligence (ChatGPT 4o) and a human quality check <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">15,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">16</ref> .

text.text: After translating, slight adjustments to several items were made to better align with natural Dutch (A5).
Face validity was checked with 28 people with lived experience: Items were tested for comprehension, clarity and interpretability, using a webform.
This resulted in minor changes for clarity.
Participants were recruited via a panel agency No Ties, targeting Dutch adults (18+) who had gambled more than once in the past 12 months.
To ensure representation across gambling products, we limited the number of participants who engaged exclusively in lotteries to a maximum of 75 17, 18 .
text.formatted: To ensure representation across gambling products, we limited the number of participants who engaged exclusively in lotteries to a maximum of 75 <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">18</ref> .

text.text: Coverage across gambling product type was assessed during data collection, with the aim of recruiting at least 50 participants per product type.
Data were collected between September and November 2025.
Participants provided active informed consent.
After the survey (15 minutes), participants were asked for a follow-up assessment (5 minutes).
A time interval of two weeks was planned between assessments to evaluate measure stability 19 .
text.formatted: A time interval of two weeks was planned between assessments to evaluate measure stability <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">19</ref> .

text.text: Panel members received gift card contribution points as a reward (2/3 Euro in value).
The study was evaluated by the Trimbos-institute ethical commission and was found to be outside of the scope of the Dutch Medical Research law.
The 26-item test version of the inventory consists of 21 items assessing frequency-based gambling harms and five items assessing event-based gambling harms (A6 and Dutch version 20 ).
text.formatted: The 26-item test version of the inventory consists of 21 items assessing frequency-based gambling harms and five items assessing event-based gambling harms (A6 and Dutch version <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">20</ref> ).

text.text: The frequency-based harm items cover eight harm domains.
Participants were asked: "Thinking about your own gambling, how often in the last 12 months has your own gambling led you to...?"

These items were rated on a 4-point scale ('never', 'sometimes', 'most of the time', '(almost) always'), capturing the frequency with which participants experienced each type of harm during the past 12 months.
The five event-based harm items assess the experience of a harmful event due to gambling in four domains: financial, relationships, work/study and crime.
These items were scored dichotomously (yes/no).
For each gambling product, participants indicated whether they had used it in the past 12 months (1), used it but more than 12 months ago (2), or never used it (3).
A product breadth score was calculated by summing the number of gambling products participants had used in the last 12 months.
This sum was subsequently dichotomised to distinguish between participants using a single gambling product (0) and those using multiple gambling products (1).
Gambling mode was derived from participants' reported engagement in land-based and online gambling activities.
Participation across products was summarised into binary variables reflecting any land-based and any online gambling (0 = no participation,1 = participation).
Participants were then classified into two categories: land-based only (0) versus (1) online only or mixed land-based/online.
Problematic gambling was assessed using the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI) 21 .
text.formatted: Problematic gambling was assessed using the Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI) <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">21</ref> .

text.text: The PGSI is a validated measure consisting of nine items that assess behavioural symptoms of gambling disorder and a few negative consequences due to gambling over the past 12 months.
Each item is rated on a 4-point scale from never (0) to (almost) always (4).
Cronbach's alpha was 0.93.
Financial wellbeing was assessed using the short version of the CBA-MI Reported Financial Wellbeing Scale 22 .
text.formatted: Financial wellbeing was assessed using the short version of the CBA-MI Reported Financial Wellbeing Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">22</ref> .

text.text: This scale captures multiple dimensions of financial wellbeing: three items focus on everyday finances, one item asks about financial outcomes related to unexpected events, and one item reflects preparedness for the future.
Responses were rated on a scale from 0 to 4, summed and then multiplied by five to obtain a score ranging from 0 (low financial wellbeing) to 100 (high financial wellbeing).
Cronbach's alpha was 0.88.
We measured personal wellbeing using 8 items of the Personal Wellbeing subscale of the Australian Unity Wellbeing Index 23 .
text.formatted: We measured personal wellbeing using 8 items of the Personal Wellbeing subscale of the Australian Unity Wellbeing Index <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">23</ref> .

text.text: These items assess satisfaction with life as a whole, standard of living, health, achievement in life, personal relationships, safety, feeling part of the community, and future security.
Responses were given on a 0-10 scale, and an overall personal wellbeing was calculated as the mean of these 8 items.
Cronbach's alpha was 0.93.
The Mental Health Inventory (MHI-5) 24 was used to measure mental health problems.
text.formatted: The Mental Health Inventory (MHI-5) <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">24</ref> was used to measure mental health problems.

text.text: The answers were scored on a 6-point scale ranging from all of the time (0) to none of the time (5).
Three items were reverse coded, such that higher scores reflect more mental health problems.
After recoding, item scores were summed and multiplied by 4 to generate a total score ranging from 0 to 100.
Cronbach's alpha was 0.88.
Prior to conducting the analyses, responses were evaluated for indications of inattentiveness to ensure data quality.
Cases were removed from the analyses when they failed both attention check items (e.g., 'Are you still there?
Enter 'most of the time' here') 25 .
text.formatted: Enter 'most of the time' here') <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">25</ref> .

text.text: For participants who failed one attention check item, cases were excluded when they showed additional indicators of inattentive responding (straight-lining with suspicious values, unusually short completion time).
Firstly, endorsement rates across answer categories were evaluated.
To assess the understandability of each harm item, participants were asked for each question whether they fully understood it.

In addition, bivariate correlations between harm items within and across domains were calculated to inform the evaluation of domain representativeness and crossdomain distinctiveness (Spearman/phi-correlations).
Convergent validity was evaluated by testing whether the harm items were associated with theoretically related gambling behaviours and wellbeing constructs.
Specifically, Spearman rank and phi-correlations were calculated to examine associations between harms and gambling behaviours, including product type engagement, product breadth and gambling mode.
Regression models were conducted to examine associations of each harm item with problematic gambling, financial wellbeing, personal wellbeing and mental health problems (in separate models).
For problematic gambling, negative binomial regression models were run, as this outcome variable is a count variable and had a highly left skewed distribution.
Linear regression models were conducted for the other outcome variables.

Because the highest response category ('(almost) always') of the harm items was infrequently endorsed, it was combined with the response category 'most of the time' in the regression analyses to avoid unstable estimates resulting from small cell counts.
Test-retest stability was assessed using weighted quadratic kappa for the frequency-based harm items and prevalence-adjusted bias-adjusted kappa (PABAK) for the event-based harm items.

To interpret the weighted quadratic kappa and PABAK, the following criteria were used: values ≤ .20 indicate poor agreement, 0.21-0.39 fair agreement, 0.40-0.59 moderate agreement, 0.60-0.79 substantial agreement and > 0.80 almost perfect agreement 26 .
text.formatted: To interpret the weighted quadratic kappa and PABAK, the following criteria were used: values ≤ .20 indicate poor agreement, 0.21-0.39 fair agreement, 0.40-0.59 moderate agreement, 0.60-0.79 substantial agreement and > 0.80 almost perfect agreement <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">26</ref> .

text.text: Because kappa statistics can be influenced by skewed distributions 27, 28 , agreement percentages were also calculated to complement the interpretation.
text.formatted: Because kappa statistics can be influenced by skewed distributions <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">28</ref> , agreement percentages were also calculated to complement the interpretation.

text.text: No missing data resulted from item non-response or dropout during survey completion.
For test-retest analyses, only participants with data available at both T0 and T1 were included.
A significance level of p < .05 was applied for all statistical tests.
text.formatted: A significance level of p < .05 was applied for all statistical tests.

text.text: To reduce the length, one frequency-based harm item per domain was selected to create a brief version of the question inventory, unless all items within a domain performed poorly.
With regard to the event-based harm items (5 items), item reduction was not applied given the limited number of items.
This study was preregistered (https://osf.io/mqb5a/overview), with some deviations.
text.formatted: This study was preregistered (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/mqb5a/overview">https://osf.io/mqb5a/overview</ref>), with some deviations.

text.text: Due to the small sample size of the advertising-recruited sample and divergent nature (T0: N = 230, T1: N = 120) the advertising sample was dropped from the current report.
Not all preregistered hypotheses and effect-size predictions were pursued due to a shift in focus toward a shortened version of the question inventory, a new objective.
The exploratory factor analysis was omitted in light of this new objective.
Feelings about gambling and help-seeking behaviour for gambling were not used as convergent validity measures.
The item about suicidality was dropped, due to lack of appropriateness in a short-form list.
Some analyses were modified because alternative approaches were considered more appropriate.
Regression analyses were employed, as these better accommodated the distributional properties of the data.
In addition, temporal stability was evaluated using agreement percentages, weighted quadratic kappa and prevalence-adjusted bias-adjusted kappa (PABAK).
Overall, 1045 participants took part in the survey at T0.
However, 68 cases were removed for failing attention checks, resulting in a final sample for analysis of 977 for T0.
In total, 841 participants participated in the follow-up survey (T1).
However, 30 participants were removed for failing attention checks, resulting in a final sample of 811 participants for T1.

text.text: To examine whether the items capture related aspects of the same construct, we assessed interitem correlations both within each domain and across domains.

Overall, correlations between the frequency-based harm items were moderate to strong (shown in Fig. 1), with the strongest correlation between borrow money and take money without asking (ρ = .82) and the weakest correlation between use savings and be absent at work/study (ρ = .41).
text.formatted: Overall, correlations between the frequency-based harm items were moderate to strong (shown in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>), with the strongest correlation between borrow money and take money without asking (ρ = .82) and the weakest correlation between use savings and be absent at work/study (ρ = .41).

text.text: Correlations between items from different domains were of similar magnitude to those within domains, or even higher.

Correlations between the event-based harm items were strong, ranging from φ = .52 to φ = .76, and showed moderate correlations with the frequency-based harms within the same domain (with the exception of a weak correlation between lost something of significant value and use savings).

To assess convergent validity, we first examined whether scores on the harm items were associated with relevant indicators of gambling behaviour.

Spearman rank correlations showed small correlations between most of the frequency-based harm items and engagement in slots, poker, casino games, betting on animal races, betting on sports and other gambling products (see Figures B1-B5 in Appendix B).

text.text: In contrast, none of the harm items were significantly correlated with participation in lotteries, scratchcards and bingo.
For the event-based harm items, phi coefficients indicated small, but significant, correlations with participation in slots, betting on animal races and other gambling products.
Exceptions were observed for the items experience abuse and big financial loss, which were not significantly associated with the use of some of those gambling products (see Figure B6 in Appendix B).

text.text: Secondly, we evaluated associations with Problematic Gambling and Wellbeing Constructs.
All items were significantly associated with problematic gambling, financial wellbeing, personal wellbeing and mental health problems (shown in Tables 3 4 5 6).

text.text: Across outcomes, a broadly consistent gradient emerged in which higher reported frequencies of a given harm were associated with a higher expected count of problematic gambling, lower levels of financial and personal wellbeing, and more mental health problems.

Note that we include the regression estimates for the event-based harm items for the sake of consistency, with the clear indicator that for the last three event-items the counts are below 5 and thus have very low observed counts.

Overall, 73 respondents provided an open-ended answer to the question whether they experienced any additional, unlisted consequences from gambling.
The majority of responses did not describe an adverse consequence experienced from gambling (including the answer 'no', n = 55).
Some referred to harms already covered by existing items or reflected alternative wording of the included harms.
Only a small number of responses (n = 11) suggested gaps, primarily related to emotional harm (i.e. feelings of guilt, regret and disappointment).
We selected items with both psychometric performance and coverage of domain content.
As all harm items showed high understandability, this criterion was not informative.
Kappa statistics were likely attenuated by low prevalences and high expected agreement.
As agreement percentages differed only marginally between items, test-retest stability was also not considered a discriminating criterion in the item selection process.

Item selection was therefore based on the conceptual representativeness and face validity of each item, supported by correlations, variability in endorsement, convergent validity, and degree of distinctiveness from other domains.
The relative importance of these criteria varied across domains, and final selections were made by considering the overall pattern of evidence rather than applying a single numerical threshold.
For the financial domain, the item assessing cut back spending on everyday items demonstrated the strongest correlations with the other financial harm items overall.
In addition, the item showed the second-highest variation in endorsement and has strong face validity.
For the personal relationship domain, the item assessing lying to family or others to hide the extent of gambling demonstrated strong face validity as a core interpersonal consequence of gambling.
This item also appeared more distinct from harms in other domains.
In addition, lying to family or others was the most commonly endorsed item within this domain.
For the mental health domain, we selected the item experiencing stress and anxiety.

The mental harm items did not differ much in item performance, but experiencing stress and anxiety has the strongest face validity as it has a wide coverage of a range of aspects associated with poorer mental health.
For physical health, the item assessing less sleep was selected.
Although less physical activity and less eating appeared somewhat more distinct due to weaker correlations with harm in other domains, less sleep has stronger face validity.
Unlike the other items, reduced sleep intuitively seems like something directly harmful at the point of experience.
In addition, less sleep showed greater variability in endorsement, suggesting better discrimination across levels of harm severity.
Extending the health domain, we included one additional item, on substance use.
Conceptually, substance use is an interplay between various factors, including the physical, mental and relationship domains, as well as environmental availability of substances.
Substances have relationships with gambling behaviour 1 (e.g. disinhibition by alcohol).
This item demonstrated good understandability and convergent validity.
The cross-domain correlations also did not show consistently stronger correlations with one domain over others.
We thus retain the single item under the heading 'other'.
To measure harm in the domain of work/study, the item assessing poor performance at work or study was selected.
Poor performance reflects a wider continuum of functional impairment, showing slightly greater variation in response patterns and slightly better convergent validity.
For the crime domain, differences in item performance between the two items were small.

Although the item taking money without asking showed substantial correlations with financial harms, conflict and neglected self-care, it was selected because of its conceptual clarity and stronger face validity compared to the item using financial resources intended for work/study to gamble.
For harm related to community relationships, none of the items was selected because, upon further consideration, these items were judged to be ambiguous and not universally applicable.
Not all individuals participate in clearly defined community groups, making it difficult to determine whether (non-)endorsement reflects gambling harm or differences in community involvement.
Besides, the item reduced contribution to community obligations could be interpreted as an opportunity cost rather than harm per se.
All five event-based harm items were retained.

A range of theoretical and empirical research documents the wide-ranging harms associated with gambling.
These harms exist across multiple domains and are wider and more extensive than the diagnostic criteria alone.
To better understand the societal burden generated from gambling, enhanced monitoring of harms is needed.
The absence of a standardised and validated Dutch-language instrument limits our ability to monitor the prevalence, nature and distribution of gambling harms across the Netherlands.
Recognising this gap, several instruments have been developed, each with different theoretical and conceptual underpinnings.
However, each has noted strengths and weaknesses.

Some, like the Short Gambling Harms Screen, disproportionately focus on certain types of harms (mainly financial), others, like the questions developed for the GSGB, have not been empirically validated.

Rather than simply adopt an existing instrument, this project worked with experts and people with lived experience of gambling harms to develop, test and validate a brief gambling harms inventory suitable for use in the Dutch context (the D-GHQI-12).

Building on prior conceptual understandings of harms, this aimed to provide broad content coverage across harm domains, be readily understandable, and demonstrate strong convergent validity and temporal stability.

Of the initial 26 items tested for potential inclusion, most had strong understandability and good convergent validity, correlating in hypothesized and expected ways with problem gambling scores, poorer financial and personal wellbeing and increased mental health issues.

These items also correlated in expected ways with participation in slots, poker, casino games, betting on animal races and sports, and other gambling products, and not with participation in lotteries, scratchcards and bingo.
Slots and casino games, in particular, have been identified as higher risk gambling activities and thus this association is commensurate with existing knowledge on product risk [30] [31] [32] .
text.formatted: Slots and casino games, in particular, have been identified as higher risk gambling activities and thus this association is commensurate with existing knowledge on product risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[30]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[32]</ref> .

text.text: Interestingly, most items did not correlate with the number of activities undertaken or product mode.

Recent research has found that engagement in particular types of gambling products, irrespective of whether they are online or land-based versions, remains associated with increased PGSI scores even when breadth of gambling involvement is taken into account.
These findings may be commensurate with that literature 32.
text.formatted: These findings may be commensurate with that literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">32</ref>.

text.text: Most items displayed good temporal stability over a multi-week time period.
The Kappa coefficients generally indicated fair to moderate agreement between measurement occasions.
However, Kappa statistics are known to be sensitive to skewed response distributions, and may underestimate agreement when the prevalence of endorsed responses is low 27, 28 .
text.formatted: However, Kappa statistics are known to be sensitive to skewed response distributions, and may underestimate agreement when the prevalence of endorsed responses is low <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">28</ref> .

text.text: Indeed, observed agreement percentages were substantially higher than kappa values alone would suggest, indicating that responses were generally stable over time.

Finally, although the questionnaire was developed around multiple domains of harm, correlations between items from different domains were often similar in magnitude to, or even stronger than, correlations within domains.
Such findings are consistent with the idea that financial, emotional, relationship, health, and other harms frequently co-occur and reinforce one another 1.
text.formatted: Such findings are consistent with the idea that financial, emotional, relationship, health, and other harms frequently co-occur and reinforce one another <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref>.

text.text: Overall, the 26 items performed well across multiple psychometric criteria.
They demonstrated high levels of understandability, generally supportive evidence for convergent validity, and satisfactory temporal stability.
The convergent validity of the items with gambling problems is in line with other harms scales 8, 33.
text.formatted: The convergent validity of the items with gambling problems is in line with other harms scales <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">33</ref>.

text.text: Based on these results, a choice of the most suitable item from each harm domain for the Brief Inventory was made based on a combination of a) retaining conceptual breadth, b) face validity, c) within domain correlations, and d) discriminatory power.
The resulting recommended items thus address limitations identified in other pre-existing screens.
For example, the Short Gambling Harm Screen (SGHS) only covers 3 of the 7 harm domains.
The GSGB questions do not include specific items on physical health.
By contrast, the D-GHQI-12 was constructed around explicit harm domains verified with international experts and Dutch stakeholders.
This ensured that most recognised domains, including crime, physical health, mental health, and financial harms, are represented by at least one item in our inventory.
Taken together, the D-GHQI-12 offers a domain-balanced, Dutch-validated tool for population monitoring.
Beyond its immediate application in the Netherlands, this work offers contributions relevant to other countries and the scientific field.
First, by making the data and materials publicly available via OSF, we facilitate adoption and adaptation of our methods and questionnaire.

Second, because the D-GHQI-12 builds on the Gambling Survey for Great Britain questions, it retains substantial item overlap with an established national survey, enabling cross-national comparison of gambling harms, something currently lacking in the field, where heterogeneous measures impede international benchmarking.
As the WHO and the Lancet Public Health Commission call for public health approaches to gambling 3 , nationally validated harm inventories such as this can be useful building blocks.
However, the measurement approach recommended by the D-GHQ-12, which separates out frequency-based harms and event-based harms, differs from many other measurement scales.

This was a deliberate design choice, recognising that some experiences are harmful irrespective of how often they occur whereas others may require cumulative experience to have equivalence. 1, 9 This approach was endorsed by our consultation with people with lived experience.
text.formatted: This was a deliberate design choice, recognising that some experiences are harmful irrespective of how often they occur whereas others may require cumulative experience to have equivalence. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">9</ref> This approach was endorsed by our consultation with people with lived experience.

text.text: This does not necessarily preclude generation of an overall scale summing each item but will require further work to understand how to score and weight different items from the frequency-response options.
There is precedent for this.
The widely used adaptation of the DSM-IV-MR for surveys attributed different weights to different diagnostic criteria 34 .
text.formatted: The widely used adaptation of the DSM-IV-MR for surveys attributed different weights to different diagnostic criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">34</ref> .

text.text: This relates to an important conceptual tension when attempting to measure harms: whether the range of harms represent a largely underlying unidimensional construct (i.e. gambling engagement resulting in harms) or whether this is a more formative construct, where gambling harms is defined by the set of topics (items) that is selected and adjustment of topics changes the nature of the construct itself. 35 The latter interpretation is not in regular use in gambling research, but it is relevant to consider, because it determines how the sum score (if produced) should be understood: as a single severity dimension, or as a structured catalogue of distinct harms experienced.
text.formatted: This relates to an important conceptual tension when attempting to measure harms: whether the range of harms represent a largely underlying unidimensional construct (i.e. gambling engagement resulting in harms) or whether this is a more formative construct, where gambling harms is defined by the set of topics (items) that is selected and adjustment of topics changes the nature of the construct itself. <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">35</ref> The latter interpretation is not in regular use in gambling research, but it is relevant to consider, because it determines how the sum score (if produced) should be understood: as a single severity dimension, or as a structured catalogue of distinct harms experienced.

text.text: Next steps to examine this could include linking the catalogue of harms to scalar changes in public health utility metrics, for instance, by weighting items according to their associated wellbeing decrements, or by administering wellbeing instruments alongside the inventory to derive population-level burden estimates.
The study has some limitations that should be noted.
First, the low prevalence of many gambling harm items may have affected the estimates.
In particular, some associations may have been disproportionately influenced by a small number of participants.
This is the nature of the sample we collected, and we recommend follow-up testing in large, gambling participantoriented samples.
Secondly, although the findings provide initial evidence for the validity and reliability of the question inventory, further validation is required in other populations.

In addition, as noted above, the inventory measures the occurrence of harms rather than their magnitude; linking harm catalogues to scalar wellbeing or utility metrics is an important direction for future work.
Finally, the inventory focuses on harms experienced by individuals who gamble themselves.
However, gambling harms extend beyond the individual and affect family members, friends and colleagues as well [36] [37] [38] .
text.formatted: However, gambling harms extend beyond the individual and affect family members, friends and colleagues as well <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[36]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[37]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[38]</ref> .

text.text: Therefore, extending harm measurement to affected others by developing a Dutch-language questionnaire for that group could be an important next step.
This study developed and evaluated the first Dutch-language inventory designed to measure gambling harms in population surveys.
The D-GHQI-12 provides a practical and comprehensive tool for assessing gambling harms across multiple domains, while remaining concise for use in large-scale surveys.
Its use may support systematic monitoring of gambling harms in the Netherlands and inform future research and public health efforts.

When using the total sample, weighted quadratic kappa values indicated moderate to substantial agreement between the two measurements (1-3.5 week interval) of the frequencybased harms (shown in Table 7).
text.formatted: When using the total sample, weighted quadratic kappa values indicated moderate to substantial agreement between the two measurements (1-3.5 week interval) of the frequencybased harms (shown in Table <ref type="table">7</ref>).

text.text: Agreement percentages were high, ranging from 86.8% to 96.7%.

When using the sample excluding participants who reported any significant change since T0, weighted quadratic kappa values were lower, indicating fair to moderate agreement, with one exception showing substantial agreement.
Percent agreements were higher (89.5% to 98.4%).

For the event-based harms, agreement was very high, with PABAK values around .94 in both the total sample as well as the subsample, and percent agreement ranging from 96.5% to 97.3% in the total sample and 97.1% to 97.6% in the subsample.
